title: A Full Reservoir, Cut Off From the Fire

place.label: University Mound Reservoir, where the Crystal Springs pipeline ended (University and Bacon streets)

hook: In 1906 the University Mound reservoir came through the earthquake almost unharmed. But the pipes leading out were cut, and its water couldn't reach the fire.
story:
In the 1880s the Spring Valley Water Company laid a 44-inch wrought-iron pipe from Crystal Springs Reservoir in San Mateo County to its new reservoir on University Mound [1]. On April 18, 1906, the earthquake broke the system in two places at once. To the south, the big pipe crossed three swamps on wooden bridges built on piles between San Bruno and San Francisco. The shaking threw sections of it four or five feet to the east and west [1]. Chief engineer Hermann Schussler later marvelled at one 800-foot length lying twisted into a 'snake-like' curve, yet showing hardly a strained seam [1].

On May 26, 1906, a reconstruction subcommittee reported that the reservoirs themselves had come through largely unharmed. But the mains leading out of College Hill and University Mound were 'completely severed', and the committee believed every serious break was in made ground. The breaks rapidly wasted the water stored in the city's reservoirs, and the districts where the main fires started were cut off completely [2]. Repair crews had to wait about ten days for scarce lumber. When it came, they rebuilt the pipe bridges with planks and flexible joints braced with wire cables made on the spot. At 7:10 a.m. on May 16, Crystal Springs water began flowing into University Mound again [1].

title: A 550-Acre Park on Paper

place.label: University Street at Mansell Street, the park's northeastern edge

hook: In 1926 San Francisco planned a park of 550 acres here and named it after John McLaren. Voters wouldn't pay for it, and the park ended up far smaller.
story:
In October 1926 the Board of Supervisors voted to take land by eminent domain for a large new public park south of Silver Avenue and east of La Grande Avenue. It was to be called Mission Park [1]. On November 29, 1926, they renamed it John McLaren Park, in thanks for the work of the city's long-serving park chief [1]. The plan was generous: 550 acres in the broad area between Alemany Boulevard, Bayshore Boulevard, Mission Street and the county line [1].

In 1927 appraisers valued every property inside the line. But the city attorney never began condemnation because there wasn't enough money, and on November 6, 1928, voters rejected a $2 million bond to buy and build the park [1]. After that the city bought land a piece at a time. The park shrank in stages to about 420 acres and then 361. Land inside the original line went to the School and Convent of the Good Shepherd, the Lick Home on University Street, two water department reservoirs, the Sunnydale housing project and Crocker Amazon Playground [1][2]. In 1946 the supervisors set the boundary at 318 acres, and the last purchases were made in 1958 [2].

title: Paintings Nailed to a Portola Garage Wall

place.label: E. R. Taylor School, 423 Burrows Street, where Longfield went to grammar school (her Portola home's address is not published)

hook: In 1949 a critic ranked her among the best new abstract painters. After her death in 2013, her canvases turned up nailed to her Portola garage wall.
story:
Zoe Golovinsky was born in San Francisco in 1924, the only child of Russian émigrés. Her father had been an aviator in the Czar's military, and he died in a work accident soon after arriving in America [1]. Her mother, a seamstress, married another émigré, Maxim Dolgopoloff. In high school Zoe changed her surname to Longfield, a loose English translation of his [1]. She went to E. R. Taylor Grammar School, Portola Junior High and Balboa High, and as a teenager she skated in figure-skating exhibitions [1][2].

After Berkeley she studied at the California School of Fine Arts under Clyfford Still, Mark Rothko and Richard Diebenkorn. She was one of the few women among the first Bay Area Abstract Expressionists [1][2]. In 1949 she and eleven of Still's students opened the cooperative Metart Gallery in a former laundry on Bush Street. A Chronicle reviewer called her one of the most successful painters working in the new style [1]. In 1951 she married and set her ambitions aside. Later she lived in her childhood home in the Portola, worked as a lithographer and graphic artist, and was often seen feeding the neighbourhood's feral cats [1]. After her death in 2013, a large collection of her paintings was found unstretched and nailed to the back wall of her garage [1].

title: Mansell Street, the Freeway That Never Came

place.label: Mansell Street at San Bruno Avenue, eastern end of the 1963 parkway

hook: Mansell Street is far wider than the streets it joins. It was built as one piece of a cross-town parkway, and the rest was never built.
story:
In January 1950 the City Planning Department proposed a parkway along Mansell Street to link McLaren Park with the Bayshore Freeway, with an extension east to Bayview Park and the bay [1]. A 1951 study grew the idea into a seven-and-a-half-mile cross-town John McLaren Parkway running from Lake Merced to Bayview Park [2]. Only one piece was built: a divided four-lane road from Brazil Avenue east to San Bruno Avenue, finished in 1963 [2]. Once Interstate 280 opened, the cross-town route was no longer needed. The city's own 1983 park plan called the road 'an unneeded anachronism' that had taken the park's flattest ridgetop land and split the park in two [2]. The plan's traffic figures showed only 1,867 cars eastbound and 2,330 westbound in a day [2].

For decades, people on foot jumped guardrails to get across, a real-life game of Frogger [3]. On November 23, 2015 the city broke ground on a $6.8 million project between University Street and Brazil Avenue; the Portola blog put the total at over $7 million. It was designed to put cars on one side of the wooded median and give the other side to people walking and cycling [3][4]. The Portola stretch, from University down to San Bruno Avenue, is part of the same 1963 road [2].

title: The Portola Boy Who Fought the Skyscrapers

place.label: San Bruno Avenue, the Portola shopping street of Duskin's boyhood

hook: He grew up shopping on San Bruno Avenue and got rich selling mini-dresses. Then he spent the money trying to stop downtown San Francisco from building upward.
story:
Alvin Duskin called himself 'a child of the Depression'. He grew up in what he called the San Bruno Avenue/Portola district, a working-class neighbourhood that he remembered as Jewish, Italian and Maltese [1]. His parents ran an apparel factory and built their house during World War II for $15,000 [1][2]. Walks to the San Bruno Avenue shops took forever, because his parents stopped 'three times in every block' to talk to people they knew [1].

Duskin went into the clothing business himself. His big idea was simple: add ten inches to a snug knit sweater and you have a mini-dress that sells for twice as much [2]. Then he turned to politics. His full-page newspaper ads helped stop a Texas developer's plan to turn Alcatraz into a tourist attraction. In 1971 he put Proposition T on the ballot, which would have banned new buildings over 72 feet unless voters approved them in advance [2]. His ad warned that the city could become 'a skyline of tombstones', and the campaign gave out 50,000 copies of a 'Vote on High-Rise Coloring Book' [2]. Proposition T lost, and so did a follow-up in 1972. But by the end of 1972 city planners had released an urban design plan controlling where towers could rise [2]. Duskin died in 2021, aged 90 [2].

title: The Diner the Neighbourhood Wouldn't Let Go

place.label: Breakfast at Tiffany's, 2499 San Bruno Avenue at Thornton Avenue

hook: When the owner of the Portola's corner diner died in 2013, the new owner planned a noodle shop. Neighbours kept asking about the diner until he changed his mind.
story:
Regular Chuck Dee remembers when this corner of San Bruno and Thornton avenues was a doughnut shop, the Pastry Express [1]. In 1978 Gerald 'Jerry' Adan took it over and ran it as Breakfast at Tiffany's, named after his niece, his sister April Martin's daughter. For 35 years he ran it from the griddle, serving what Dee called 'truck-stop style food, but with fresher ingredients' and loud politics [1]. Adan died of cancer in September 2013. Martin hoped to take over, but the building's elderly owner refused to renew the lease and put it up for sale; Martin pasted a goodbye note on the window [1][2][3].

Kash Feng, a Portola resident who owned several Japanese restaurants, bought the building that October. He planned to open a Northern Chinese noodle-and-dumpling shop [1]. But while he gutted the space, neighbours he had never seen kept stopping by to ask whether 'Tiffy's' was coming back. Jack Tse, then the Portola Neighborhood Association's corridor manager, told him that reopening the diner would guarantee success [1]. Partway through the remodel Feng changed his plans, and the city's SF Shines program helped pay for paint and a new sign [1]. He kept only the old counter, ordered swivel seats from the East Coast, and reopened on November 1, 2014, to a line out the door [1].

title: Goats, Parrots and a Hawk on Woolsey Hill

place.label: Woolsey Street side of University Mound Reservoir's South Basin

hook: One August morning in 2012 a truck unloaded 275 goats onto the reservoir slopes. They were there to eat the brush and cut the fire risk.
story:
On the morning of August 2, 2012, a truck unloaded 275 goats onto the Woolsey Street side of University Mound Reservoir's South Basin [1]. The mixed herd of Angora, Pygmy, Alpine and Spanish goats came from a company called Goats R Us. With a goatherd and a dog, they were to spend a few days eating the brush on the steep slopes to reduce the fire risk, as part of the water department's integrated pest management program [1]. Jerilyn Downing, the department's landscape manager, said the goats were hired once a year for sites across the city: about 300 more were at Twin Peaks, and roughly 1,000 were working citywide [1]. Two weeks later a flock turned up at College Hill Reservoir in Bernal Heights. A new neighbour there worked out that they belonged to the same SF Water brush-clearance project that had 'recently devoured the tall grasses of the Portola District' [2].

The hill has wilder residents too. In 2017 neighbours reported a flock of wild parrots, apparently cherry-headed conures, living in the trees between Woolsey Street and the north end of Burton High School. Neighbours said the birds flew off toward downtown in the morning and came back in the late afternoon. A block away, near Goettingen and Dwight streets, a hawk had built a nest [3].

title: A Buried Creek Beneath Wayland Street

place.label: Wayland Street near University Street, along the proposed Upper Yosemite Creek daylighting route

hook: A creek rises in McLaren Park and runs to the bay, mostly in a pipe under Portola streets. In 2013 the city began planning to bring part back above ground.
story:
Yosemite Creek rises from a spring in McLaren Park and once ran downhill all the way to the bay [1][2]. Today most of it flows through a covered pipe under the Portola's streets and into the city's combined sewer system. On a dry day that system treats about 80 million gallons of water; in a heavy rain it can be 575 million [1]. An early Portola resident, in oral histories gathered by Chris Ortiz, recalled a creek by his house near Mansell Street, 'probably Yosemite Cr.' [3].

In the autumn of 2013 the Public Utilities Commission led a packed crowd of neighbours along the route of its Upper Yosemite Creek Daylighting project, a plan to bring part of the creek back to the surface along McLaren Park's border with the Portola [1]. One idea was to move back the reservoir fence and let the creek wind down beside the basin through a new public space [1]. Project manager Raphael Garcia said that if it succeeded it would be the city's first daylighting project of its kind. Asked for money to take it further, he said: 'the funds I have, are the funds I have' [1]. In March 2017 the final design, with the creek drawn along Wayland Street, was shown at a church hall on Woolsey Street [2].

title: A Brewery Comes to San Bruno Avenue

place.label: Ferment Drink Repeat taproom, 2636 San Bruno Avenue

hook: Plans for San Bruno Avenue's first brewery took 16 months just to get permits and money. On opening night the taproom was full until closing.
story:
When a start-up called Ferment Drink Repeat announced plans for San Bruno Avenue's first brewery. In October 2015 several neighbours emailed the local blog asking for news, so its writer asked the owners directly [1]. Their answer: they had spent 16 months getting building permits and funding in place, about 12 months longer than they had hoped, and had only just received the approval letter for the loan they needed to build [1]. They wouldn't guess at an opening date, because projects 'seem to have a habit of falling behind schedule' [1]. A reader noted that nothing had changed at the storefront [1].

By April 2016 they were at least selling home-brewing supplies in the space. Co-owner Kevin helped a blogger choose a first batch, a Little Bitty Brown Ale, which ended up bubbling in a bucket in his office [2]. The taproom at 2636 San Bruno Avenue finally had a soft opening on May 25, 2016, almost two and a half years after the project began, and it stayed full until closing [3]. Co-owner Shae kept thanking the neighbourhood for backing them through the city approvals. The blog's writer was glad of a reason to be on the main street after 3 p.m. [3]. A year later the brewery marked its first anniversary with live music all day [4].

title: No High-Pressure Hydrants for the Portola

place.label: Silver Avenue at University Street, on the proposed route of a high-pressure fire main to University Mound Reservoir

hook: After 1906 San Francisco built an emergency firefighting water network that never reached the Portola. By 2016 the proposed substitute was fifteen miles of hose.
story:
After the 1906 disaster, a city committee called for a separate high-pressure fire main system supplied with water pumped from the bay. It was meant only for the 'congested value district' downtown [2]. The resulting Auxiliary Water Supply System was finished by 1913 and never reached many outer neighbourhoods, the Portola among them [1].

Between 2010 and 2012, Public Utilities Commission maps showed an extension running along Geneva and Silver avenues to University Mound Reservoir, the Portola's 140-million-gallon hilltop basin [1]. The agency's later plans dropped it. Instead it floated a 'Flexible Water Supply System': about 15 miles of 12-inch hose stored at the Sunset and University Mound reservoirs, which volunteers from the Neighborhood Emergency Response Team would lay out after an earthquake. Critics warned of debris-blocked, pitch-dark streets, and the plan was abandoned [1]. On April 6, 2016, firefighters' union president Thomas O'Connor wrote to Supervisor Aaron Peskin that the union was 'greatly disturbed' that the Silver Avenue extension and others were being dropped. At a hearing on March 15, 2017, Peskin wondered aloud whether the city should 'bite the bullet' on a half-billion-dollar investment [1]. By then only University Mound's North Basin had been seismically upgraded, in 2010 [1].

title: A Mudslide Stairway Becomes a Hillside Garden

place.label: Goettingen Street stairway and garden at Dwight Street

hook: The slope beside the Goettingen Street steps used to be a dirt pile full of dumped rubbish. Neighbours spent ten years turning it into a garden with a lookout.
story:
About ten years before 2018, the slope beside the Goettingen Street stairs was a mud slide and a dumping ground. The Portola's neighbourhood blog later called it 'a garbage covered dirt pile' [1][3]. Neighbours on the 700 block of Goettingen formed the Goettingen Neighbors Group and started clearing it [1]. By 2015 the group had members from as far away as Hamilton and Colby streets. That September they spent a whole Saturday sweeping, weeding, hauling rubbish and laying donated slate flagstones ahead of the annual Portola Garden Tour [1].

In 2016 the group tried to win a Parks Alliance grant in an online vote for 'Goettingen Cascades'. Portola artist Phillip Hua designed it as a glass and ceramic 'waterway' that would shimmer and even glow as it ran down through the garden at Dwight and Goettingen. The group also held a plant sale to raise money [2]. In summer 2018 work finally began. Paid for by neighbours and city Community Challenge Grants, crews poured a board-formed concrete platform halfway up the stairs, with built-in benches and a view north toward downtown. A tile mosaic on the steps was planned as the next phase [3].
